Post-mastectomy immunosuppression

In a 19-person post-surgical pilot, selected immune markers moved toward reference levels and fewer losses were reported on days 1 and 8 in the light group. The trial did not measure infection prevention or cancer recurrence.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In a 19-person post-surgical pilot, selected immune markers moved toward reference levels and fewer losses were reported on days 1 and 8 in the light group. The trial did not measure infection prevention or cancer recurrence.

Summary of the Evidence

One unique human controlled pilot studied post-surgical immunorehabilitation in 19 breast-cancer patients. The publication reports random assignment to active or sham/control groups, although the database labels the design non-randomized; the article's allocation description is used here. This is one small study, not evidence of prevention of infection or cancer recurrence. No animal or standalone laboratory study was identified for this indication.

Human and clinical evidence

Zhevago and colleagues treated 11 patients and compared them with eight controls after mastectomy. Selected immune markers were closer to reference values and fewer reductions in measured parameters were reported on days 1 and 8. These are laboratory surrogate outcomes. The study did not establish fewer postoperative infections, improved cancer control, or longer survival (Zhevago et al. 2017).

Animal evidence

No relevant animal study was identified in this category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate cell or ex-vivo study specific to post-mastectomy immunosuppression was identified. Immune-marker measurements in the patient study are not an additional laboratory experiment.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The intervention was polychromatic light spanning 480 to 3400 nm, covering visible and infrared light without ultraviolet, with 95% polarization. The database reports 40 mW/cm² irradiance and 24 J/cm² fluence applied to the sacral area for seven days, beginning the day after surgery. This localized regimen and short follow-up do not establish effects for other devices, treatment areas, or clinical endpoints.

Interpretation

The pilot provides a preliminary signal in selected immune markers after surgery. It does not demonstrate a clinical reduction in infection or cancer outcomes, and the small sample requires replication with those outcomes measured directly.

Evidence strength in source summarySelected immune markers in the first week after breast-cancer surgery: Very low Clinical infection or cancer outcomes: No direct evidence identified
Publications and records1 unique title

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One 19-person controlled pilot measured immune markers after surgery and reported differences over the first eight days. The study is small and does not show fewer infections, cancer recurrence, or another clinical outcome. Replication with prespecified clinical endpoints and a clearly reported allocation method is needed before inferring patient-level benefit.
